Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette: The assault happened on a humid Tuesday night after her shift ended, leaving her stranded at a dimly lit transit stop. She has never managed to stitch the moments together; her mind holds only fractured snapshots—a flash of a dark uniform, the sudden pressure of a hand on her wrist, the sharp, metallic taste of copper and rain, and the distant, rising wail of an ambulance that arrived too late. When the memory surfaces now, it does not arrive as a story but as a sudden, physical reoccupation of the past, so vivid that ordinary recollections of her wedding day feel flat by comparison. She has learned to steer clear of the narrative. If she allows herself to think about the event, she is certain she will not be able to handle it, so she keeps the pieces buried, knowing they will only surface when stress fractures her composure. Over the following months, the world around her became a landscape of potential threats. Linh developed a habit of scanning for exits the moment her foot crossed any threshold, her eyes darting to windows and stairwells before she even hung up her bag. In her call center cubicle, vigilance became a full-time occupation. She watched her coworkers’ hands and expressions, searching for danger, and whenever a sudden movement occurred behind her—a colleague leaning over to check a script—her body reacted as if she were back at that stop, muscles locking and breath catching. She had come to believe she had to be on guard all the time, a conviction that left her shoulders permanently raised. To manage the mounting tension, she turned to private, physical releases. When the pressure became too heavy, she would retreat to the bathroom, discharging anxiety through sexual fantasies and activity, a routine that temporarily quieted the noise but left her feeling hollow afterward. The avoidance habits formed gradually, layering over her daily life until they dictated her movements. She stopped engaging when coworkers mentioned the assault, shifting conversations away with forced lightness. She could not be around people in authority or uniform without a cold knot forming, so she kept her head down, averted her gaze from her supervisor’s tie, and changed her routes to bypass security patrols. Stress at work acted as a direct conduit to her trauma responses; the moment her call volume spiked, the old fear returned, and she instinctively pulled away from anyone who asked how she was coping. In her marital home, seeing happy families walking in the park or a colleague’s wedding photos made her chest tighten with inadequacy. She was newly married, and she had come to believe she was inadequate to the life she had chosen, convinced her fractured mind meant she would never be whole enough to be a good wife. The tipping point arrived when the weight of staying perpetually alert began to fracture her marriage. Her husband noticed how she flinched at doorbells, how she would lie awake replaying the copper-and-rain taste of that night, and how the private coping had become an exhausting ritual. The realization that she could not outrun the fear any longer brought her to the clinic. She sits now in the intake room, her fingers tracing the doorframe as her eyes automatically catalog the exits. She hopes someone might teach her how to step off the watch, to let her mind rest without the terror of shattering. What frightens her most is that she will always be waiting for the siren to wail or the stress to crack her open, leaving her stranded in a past she can neither piece together nor escape.
